aspect: EXAMPLE - the size, and the turn
description: Mexico received $61.79bn in family remittances in 2025, a 4.6% year-on-year fall - the first annual contraction after eleven consecutive years of growth and the biggest drop since 2009. The record was 2024 at $64.7bn across 164.8m transactions.

aspect: EXAMPLE - what it is worth to the country
description: Remittances were about 3.4% of Mexican GDP in 2025. Guanajuato was the largest recipient state at $5.51bn, 8.9% of the national total. Electronic transfer accounted for 99.1%.
energy_note: Three and a half per cent of the economy, sent home in pieces.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the money shrank even where it arrived
description: The peso appreciated 10.2% against the dollar between November 2024 and November 2025; with inflation, the real purchasing power of remittances fell 14.4% year-on-year in November for 4.4m receiving households.
energy_note: Same dollars, a seventh less food.

aspect: The fee is a tax on being poor and far away
description: Transfer costs fall hardest on small, frequent transfers, which is the pattern used by people sending part of a weekly wage.
money_note: Annual fees on regular small transfers.
energy_note: Charged most per dollar for sending the fewest.

aspect: Sending it is also how he stays a father
description: The transfer is the relationship: it is proof of continued presence, and missing one is read at home as something other than a bad month.
energy_note: The month he sends nothing means something else entirely.

aspect: The 2025 fall is an enforcement indicator
description: Analysts attributed much of the drop to US immigration policy change, with DHS data suggesting border crossings down 93% year-on-year in 2025. The remittance line is therefore a proxy for how many men are managing to be there at all.
energy_note: The money falling is the men not arriving.
